item.title: Everyone Was Making TikToks and Dalgona Coffee. I Wanted to Make Something Else.
item.dc:creator: Rajat Rai
item.content:encoded:
A story about Jhatpat, the ideas we had, how close we came, and what I learned along the way.

Remember when everyone was making TikToks, trying dalgona coffee, and suddenly, the internet was full of Rasode Mein Kaun Tha memes? Those were some strange times.

I was in my first year of college when COVID happened. During our second semester, classes moved online, colleges shut down, and suddenly, we were all sitting at home, attending lectures through our laptops. Nobody really knew how long this would last or when things would go back to normal.

But the internet was busy doing its own thing. Trends came and went, people found new ways to entertain themselves, and brands were trying to figure out how to be part of these conversations.

I was already on Twitter, but around that time, I also joined Instagram. I wanted to see what was happening there and what people were creating. Looking back, I’m still not entirely sure whether joining Instagram was a good decision. Haha.

Somewhere around this time, my friends and I started talking about the things we were seeing online. We noticed how trends were becoming a way for brands to reach people, and we wondered if we could do something around it ourselves.

I didn’t have a grand business plan or some big vision of becoming an entrepreneur. I was in my first year of college. I just wanted to try something of my own, make something with my friends, and see if we could take an idea beyond our conversations.

We didn’t know much about running a business, and we certainly didn’t have everything figured out. But we had some ideas, we were excited about them, and we wanted to see where they could take us.

And that’s how Jhatpat began.

Jhatpat: An Idea That Came Together, Well, Jhatpat

We started discussing what we could actually do with the idea. We were interested in social media, the trends people were talking about, and how brands could use them to reach people. Moment marketing was something we wanted to explore, and we thought we could build something around it.

We needed a name, too. And as you might have guessed, we came up with Jhatpat pretty jhatpat. There wasn’t a long brainstorming session or some deep thought behind it. We liked the name, agreed on it, and moved on.

We wanted to create content around things people were talking about and eventually help brands reach their audiences through it. But before approaching clients, we needed something that showed what we could create.

That’s where School Diaries by Jhatpat came in.

It was an audio drama based on school memories and first love. We wanted to tell a story people could connect with, and it could also give potential clients an idea of the kind of content we were capable of making.

I took up almost everything that went into making it. I wrote the script, directed it, narrated it, and edited the audio.

I don’t think I fully understood what I was getting myself into. I just wanted to make it happen.

At that point, we were figuring things out as we went along. We had an idea for Jhatpat, and now we had a project we could create and share with people.

It was time to see if we could bring it to life.

School Diaries: Our First Real Creation

The first thing we launched under Jhatpat was School Diaries, an audio drama about school memories and first love.

We planned to make 12 episodes. At the time, that felt like a reasonable plan. We had a story to tell, ideas to explore, and a team willing to give it a shot.

We were doing this for the first time, so there was a lot to figure out. We didn’t have years of experience behind us. We were learning as we went, from writing and recording to editing the audio and putting everything together.

What I remember most is seeing an idea gradually take shape. Something that had started as a conversation was becoming an actual story that people could listen to.

Then we released the first episode, and the response was really good.

Friends reached out. Even relatives got in touch. People told us how the story reminded them of their own school days. It felt good to know that something we had created could bring back memories for other people.

For a bunch of college students trying to create something of their own, that response meant a lot. We had made something, put it out into the world, and people connected with it.

But getting the first episode out was one thing. Keeping the series going was another.

We had planned 12 episodes, but we ended up making only five. The series came to an abrupt end as we lost direction and the enthusiasm to keep producing it. We also lacked the skills and experience to turn that initial response into something sustainable.

Looking back, I don’t think I fully understood what it would take to keep a project going. Getting people excited about the first episode wasn’t enough. We needed to keep planning, coordinate with everyone, and consistently put in the work.

We hadn’t quite figured out how to do that.

Still, School Diaries remains one of the most memorable parts of the Jhatpat journey for me. We didn’t finish what we had planned, but we made something and saw people respond to it. That experience was worth a lot.

We Were Building Together, Miles Apart

One thing I still find interesting about Jhatpat is that we were building it while being in different parts of India.

We weren’t sitting together in a room, discussing ideas over coffee or working from the same office. We were relying on the internet to get things done.

This was during COVID, so working remotely wasn’t really a choice. It was simply how we had to work.

Most of our coordination happened over WhatsApp, online meetings, and shared documents. We’d discuss ideas, divide the work, and try to bring everything together without being physically present with one another.

For me, it was one of the first times I experienced how technology could bring people together to build something. We didn’t need to be in the same place to get started. We could work on an idea together, even from different parts of the country.

That experience stayed with me. Technology made it possible for us to collaborate despite the distance, and we were learning how to use it to make something together.

Of course, being able to work together and actually working well together were two different things. We were about to learn that part, too.

We Wanted to Build Everything

Doing everything at once doesn’t mean you’re making progress. Sometimes, it just means you’re spreading yourself too thin.

School Diaries was just one part of what we wanted to do with Jhatpat. We had started with content, but I wanted to explore how we could turn it into something bigger.

The idea was to help brands with moment marketing. We could create content around things people were talking about and use our pages and audio shows to promote products. We also wanted to build a website and explore other formats.

There was a lot we wanted to do. In hindsight, probably too much for a team that was still figuring out how to get its first project off the ground.

Whenever we discussed something new, it felt like another opportunity worth exploring. We’d talk about ideas, plan how they could work, and imagine what Jhatpat could eventually become. But we didn’t always spend enough time figuring out how we would actually execute them.

We also started thinking about hiring people. We wanted audio artists, marketing interns, and others who could help us take things forward. We even brought in an HR person who did a good job helping us with the hiring process.

The thing was, we were still figuring out what Jhatpat would become. We were bringing people on board while we were still working out our direction, what we wanted to focus on, and how everything would fit together.

Hiring people was one thing. Knowing what to do with the resources we had was another.

We weren’t entirely sure how to manage the people we brought in, organise their work, or make sure everyone was moving in the same direction. We were trying to build a team while we were still figuring out the business ourselves.

Then college started reopening. The circumstances that had allowed us to spend so much time experimenting during lockdown were changing. Everyone had other things to focus on, and keeping Jhatpat moving became harder.

Looking back, I think I was confusing activity with progress. We were discussing ideas, making plans, exploring possibilities, and bringing people on board. But we weren’t consistently turning those plans into something real.

At the time, I didn’t see all of this clearly. I just knew there was a lot we wanted to do, but things weren’t moving the way I had imagined.

And then we got close to something that could have taken Jhatpat a step further.

We Were Getting Close

At one point, it felt like Jhatpat might actually turn into a business.

We had started reaching out to potential clients with the idea of creating ads for brands and featuring them through our content, social media pages, and audio shows.

We pitched a few brands. I can’t name them now, but one of them was a big name in the school accessories space.

We shared our proposal, and they asked us to share our pricing. We worked on the pricing and sent it across. The next step was supposed to be a meeting where we could discuss things further.

For us, this was a big deal. We were college students trying to build something of our own, and here was a brand considering what we had to offer.

Until then, we had mostly been experimenting with our own ideas. Now, there was a possibility that someone might pay us to create something for them.

I don’t remember treating it like some huge milestone at the time. We were simply trying to make things work. But looking back, I think getting that far was encouraging.

Of course, sending a proposal and pricing wasn’t the same as having a client. There was still a meeting to be had and more to discuss. I don’t know whether it would have turned into a deal.

What I do remember is that we had managed to take a potential opportunity a few steps further than just talking about an idea.

I sometimes wonder what would have happened next.

Friends Are Not Automatically a Team

At some point, I had to accept that Jhatpat wasn’t going the way I had imagined.

We had created School Diaries, explored moment marketing, discussed a website, started hiring, and even taken a potential client opportunity a few steps further. But there was a gap between everything we wanted to do and what we were actually getting done.

We were trying to do too many things at once. Deadlines were being missed, ideas weren’t moving forward, and we were struggling to maintain the enthusiasm we had at the beginning.

College was reopening, everyone had other things going on, and we hadn’t figured out how to manage our work properly.

I could see that things weren’t working, but I didn’t have a clear solution either.

I had a lot of ideas in my head, but I struggled to explain them in a way that everyone could work with. I could imagine what Jhatpat might become, but turning that picture into a clear plan, with specific tasks and expectations, was much harder than I had expected.

I also had to understand something about working with friends.

When you start something with your friends, it’s easy to assume that everyone will be equally excited about it. You already know each other, you enjoy spending time together, and you think that should make working together easier.

Sometimes it does. But being friends doesn’t automatically mean you have the same priorities or want to put in the same amount of time and effort.

And that’s okay. People have their own lives, interests, and plans. Not everyone has to be as invested in an idea as the person who started it.

I don’t think the problem was simply that my friends weren’t enthusiastic enough. I also hadn’t figured out how to lead a team. I didn’t know how to set clear expectations, communicate what needed to be done, or help everyone work towards the same goal.

We were friends trying to build something together, but we hadn’t really learned how to become a team.

Eventually, I decided that it was time to end Jhatpat. I spoke to the others about it, and we agreed to call it a day. I wanted to take some time before trying something new, perhaps with a different team or a different approach.

It wasn’t easy to walk away from something we’d spent so much time thinking about and working on. We had created something we were proud of, explored ideas, and come close to opportunities that might have gone somewhere. I still don’t know what would have happened if we’d continued.

But I also knew that coming up with more ideas wasn’t going to solve the problems we were facing. Before trying to build something again, I needed to understand what I had done wrong and what I needed to learn.

As the person who started Jhatpat, I had to accept my part in it. I had the ideas, but I hadn’t yet learned how to turn them into a plan that other people could understand and work towards.

I was still learning what it meant to build something with other people. Jhatpat ended before I had figured that out.

What I See in Jhatpat Today

Looking back, I think the most disappointing part of Jhatpat was that we never really found out what it could have become.

We started with an idea during COVID. We created School Diaries, got a good response to our first episode, explored different things, and even took our moment marketing idea a few steps further with potential clients.

I was disappointed. Not because I thought we were guaranteed to succeed, but because I had imagined taking it further, and we never really got there.

Sometimes I wonder what would have happened if we had focused on one thing, worked with a different team, or understood a little more about what we were doing. Maybe things would have turned out differently. Maybe they wouldn’t have. I don’t think I’ll ever know.

It’s also interesting to look back at the things we were trying to do. Moment marketing, audio storytelling, and creating content for brands are all things we see around us today. I sometimes wonder whether we had spotted an opportunity without really understanding how to turn it into a business.

But I don’t want to pretend that we were ahead of our time or that Jhatpat would have succeeded if only we had continued. We had a lot to learn, and we learned some of it the hard way.

Jhatpat was my first attempt at building something of my own. It taught me that having ideas and being excited about them is one thing. Choosing what to focus on, communicating clearly, and doing the work consistently is something else.

I still wish we had taken it further. But I also know that ending it was a decision I made because I wanted to step back and try again with a different approach.

We didn’t build what we had imagined when we started Jhatpat. We tried to build something of our own, learned along the way, and never quite found out how far we could have taken it.

And perhaps that’s what I’ll remember most about Jhatpat.

If you’d like to hear what we made, you can listen to School Diaries here. We planned 12 episodes, made five, and the last episode never came. Maybe someday. 🎧

item.title: Understanding Dharma: Why Every Choice Matters
item.dc:creator: Rajat Rai
item.content:encoded:
Dharma is not religion, rules or rituals. It is the responsibility of being true to one’s nature while acting consciously in the world.

Have you ever been stuck between two choices, both which felt right and wrong at the same time ?

One path promises peace but demands sacrifice. The other offers comfort but leaves a quite sense of guilt. This inner conflict has a name in the Indian Philosophy. It’s called Dharma Sankat. It is a moment where the life doesn’t ask what is easy or rewarding, but what is right. To win over this conflict our scriptures prescribes us to understand Dharma.

What is Dharma ?

When conversations like this moves beyond India, Dharma is often translated as religion, duty or morality. These words approach its meaning but never quite arrive.

Dharma refuses to fit into a single English equivalent, not because the idea is vague, but because its expensive. It describes a relationship between self, society and circumstances, shaping how we act when certainty dissolves.

The word Dharma is derived from the Sanskrit root Dhṛ, meaning to hold, support, or sustain. From it comes Dharan, that which upholds the very structure of life.

Dharma, therefore, is not merely believed or followed. It is when the sustaining principles of our universe are consciously imbibed and lived, they become Dharma.

Dharma Beyond Religion and Rules

If Dharma were a fixed rulebook, it would have had a single, universally agreed definition. Instead, across time and thinkers, Dharma has been explained in different way. They each emphasize a different dimension of the same truth. Let’s see a few of them.

Premanand Maharaj often describes Dharma as conduct aligned with the scriptures, where right action naturally leads to satkarma and inner peace. In this view, Dharma is not enforced but it rewards itself by bringing harmony to life.

Here, Dharma functions as a moral alignment: live rightly, and happiness follows; not as pleasure, but as stability.

Sadhguru approaches Dharma as law and not belief, but the natural order that governs human interactions and life itself. Just as physical laws operate whether we believe in them or not, Dharma functions as a social and existential law that sustains balance.

This understanding shifts Dharma away from faith and toward functionality.

J Sai Deepak draws a crucial distinction: Dharma is not faith. Faith asks for belief without questioning; Dharma, rooted in this civilization, encourages inquiry, debate, and reasoning.
At the same time, he points out that Dharma can still be religious in nature because it provides the ethical and cultural foundation upon which rights, duties, and even constitutional frameworks are built.

Dharma here is civilizational order, not blind belief.

Ami Ganatra defines Dharma simply and powerfully as that which sustains. Any action, value, or system that supports life, harmony, and continuity aligns with Dharma. Anything that destroys balance, no matter how justified it appears, move away from it.

This view brings Dharma back to its etymological root: that which holds together.

Swami Chinmayananda offers perhaps the most elegant explanation: Dharma is the essential property of a being.

Just as sweetness is the essential nature of sugar and fire cannot exist without heat. Dharma is the inner nature that defines right action for a person. When one acts against this essential nature, suffering follows not as punishment, but as consequence.

This understanding makes Dharma deeply personal and experiential.

Dharma may be seen as scriptural guidance, social law, civilizational responsibility, or the principle that sustains life, yet at its core it is the essential nature expressed through action. Though explained in many ways, its purpose remains the same, to uphold life, order, and meaning through conscious choice.

Dharma and Karma: Choice and Consequence

Dharma and Karma are often spoken of together, yet they are frequently misunderstood as separate ideas. Dharma is assumed to be about what is right, while Karma is seen as reward or punishment. In reality, they are part of the same movement. Dharma guides the choice, and Karma carries the consequence of that choice forward.

In modern life, people are often encouraged to “just do your karma” or “focus on action, not outcome.” While this sounds empowering, it is incomplete. Action without rightness is not freedom; it is momentum. When Karma is disconnected from Dharma, action may produce results, but it also produces restlessness, confusion, and inner conflict.

Think of a moment when you chose the easier truth instead of the honest one. Maybe it was in a conversation with family, a relationship, or even with yourself. Nothing dramatic. Just a small adjustment to avoid discomfort. It worked. The situation passed. No consequences followed immediately.

The next time, the adjustment came faster. You learned where to soften words, where to stay silent, where to bend the story so life stayed smooth. Slowly, without noticing, the choice stopped feeling like a choice. It became a habit.

Over time, the effort shifted from being real to being careful. You began carrying unspoken explanations, half-truths, and inner justifications. Outwardly, life continued. Inwardly, a quiet unease settled in. Not because something terrible happened, but because something honest was left behind.

That habit shaped how you saw yourself. And how you saw yourself shaped the life you moved into. Not as punishment, but as consequence. The restlessness, the fatigue, the feeling that something was always slightly off came not from action itself, but from action taken without Dharma.

Karma moved, results appeared, but peace did not. And that absence was the real signal.

Karma does not judge. It records. Every action leaves an imprint on the mind, the environment, and the self. Repeated actions turn into habits. Habits slowly shape identity. Identity, lived long enough, becomes destiny. This is why Karma is not fate, and Dharma is not moral advice. Together, they describe how life responds to conscious or unconscious choices.

Dharma gives direction to action, and Karma gives continuity to its effects. When action is aligned with Dharma, Karma becomes growth rather than bondage. When action ignores Dharma, Karma binds not because it is cruel, but because it is precise.

Which is why, Dharma and Karma are not ancient ideas meant for scriptures alone. They are living principles that quietly shape everyday life, whether one believes in them or not.

Why Dharma and Karma Bind Humans ?

Dharma and Karma bind only humans because only humans possess the capacity to choose consciously. A tree gives shade without intention, a river flows without preference, and an animal acts by instinct. They act, but they do not deliberate. Humans alone pause, evaluate, desire, justify, and regret. This capacity for conscious choice is what gives rise to both freedom and bondage.

Karma becomes binding not because of action itself, but because of attachment to outcomes, fear of loss, craving for validation, and identification with results. When action is driven by expectation rather than awareness, Karma tightens into Bandhan. Dharma is what loosens that grip by aligning action with clarity rather than compulsion.

This is why Krishna does not ask Arjuna to renounce action, but to refine the mind with Yogastha Buddhi. Yogastha Buddhi is a state of steady intelligence where one remains anchored while acting. It is action performed with involvement but without inner disturbance, where success and failure no longer shake the sense of self. Such a mind acts fully, yet remains free.

When Dharma is absent, Karma binds. When Dharma is present, Karma becomes a means of growth. The difference lies not in what is done, but in the inner condition from which it is done.

This inner condition is explained beautifully by Swami Tejomayananda, who describes Dharma through ten essential characteristics that refine human conduct and awareness.

Dhriti is patience, the capacity to remain steady under pressure rather than react impulsively.
Kshama is forgiveness, not weakness, but the strength to release resentment.
Damah is self-restraint, the ability to govern impulses instead of being driven by them.
Asteya is non-stealing, which includes not taking what is not earned, whether material, emotional, or intellectual.
Shaucha is cleanliness, not only of the body, but of thoughts and intentions.
Indriya Nigraha is control of the senses, ensuring that perception does not turn into addiction.
Dhi is benevolent intellect, the ability to think clearly and compassionately.
Vidya is spiritual knowledge, the understanding of one’s deeper nature beyond roles and achievements.
Satyam is love of truth, not merely speaking it, but living it.
Akrodha is freedom from anger, the refusal to let rage dictate action.

These qualities are not moral decorations. They are inner disciplines that prevent Karma from turning into bondage. They prepare the mind to act without being enslaved by action.

And that is why, Dharma and Karma are not external systems imposed on humans. They arise from the very structure of human consciousness. Karma binds when awareness is absent, and Dharma liberates when awareness is present. This is why the same action can either imprison or free, depending entirely on the mind behind it.

Vidura and Krishna on Swadharma

Swadharma is the Dharma that arises from one’s own nature, position, capacity, and stage of life. It is not chosen arbitrarily, nor imposed externally. It unfolds naturally from who one is and what the moment demands. Because this principle does not change with time, geography, or circumstance, Swadharma is inseparable from Sanatan Dharma. Sanatan means eternal, and Dharma is eternal precisely because the responsibility to act consciously has always belonged to human life. What changes is the form of action, not the principle behind it.

Sanatan Dharma is therefore not a fixed code, but an eternal framework within which Swadharma operates. It is the timeless truth that right action must be aligned with one’s conscience, role, and responsibility. When Swadharma is lived sincerely, Sanatan Dharma expresses itself in the present moment.

This clarity is articulated powerfully by Vidura in the Mahabharata. Vidura explains Dharma as a widening circle of responsibility, where the smaller must sometimes yield to protect the larger. An individual may be set aside for the sake of the family, the family for the sake of the village, the village for the sake of the nation, and everything for the sake of the soul, the Dharma itself. Dharma, in this sense, is not guided by emotional attachment but by conscious prioritization of what sustains life and order.

Vidura’s perspective shows that Dharma is rooted in conscience and wisdom, not convenience. It calls for sacrifice, but never blind sacrifice. What is relinquished is determined by clarity about what truly needs protection, not by fear, preference, or personal gain.

The same truth is conveyed by Krishna on the battlefield of Kurukshetra. Arjuna’s confusion is not about violence or peace, but about abandoning his Swadharma as a warrior out of emotional overwhelm. Krishna does not ask Arjuna to suppress compassion, nor does he glorify war. He reminds Arjuna that escaping one’s Swadharma does not lead to righteousness, but to inner collapse. To act according to another’s Dharma, however noble it may appear, leads to fear and confusion.

Krishna emphasizes that true Dharma is to abide by one’s conscience with clarity and steadiness. Action must be performed, but without attachment, hatred, or ego. This is why Dharma is flexible in expression but firm in essence. It adapts to circumstances so that life may be sustained, not fractured. Dharma is not rigidity, and it is not freedom without responsibility. It is balance.

This understanding is captured in the timeless principle, dharma rakshati dharma. When Dharma is protected through conscious action, Dharma in turn protects the individual and society. When it is compromised for comfort or fear, the same Dharma withdraws its support.

In this way, Swadharma and Sanatan Dharma are not two separate ideas. They are one continuous truth, lived personally and upheld universally, reminding humans that freedom without conscience leads to chaos, and duty without awareness leads to bondage.

Dharma Sankat: When Right Confronts Right

A Dharma Sankat arises not when one must choose between good and bad, but when one is forced to choose between two competing responsibilities, both of which feel morally valid. It is the most human of crises, because it demands not obedience, but wisdom.

History offers powerful illustrations of this inner conflict. Karna stands torn between gratitude to Duryodhana and loyalty to truth, knowing that either choice would betray a part of himself. Rama faces exile not because he lacks power to resist, but because upholding his father’s word sustains a larger moral order. Yudhishthira struggles between truth and compassion, discovering that rigid righteousness can itself become a form of adharma. These figures were not confused about right and wrong; they were burdened by the cost of choosing one right over another.

What makes these moments timeless is that the form of Dharma Sankat has changed, but its essence has not. Today, the battlefield is quieter and the stakes appear personal, yet the conflict remains the same. A professional stays silent in the face of unethical practices to protect a livelihood. A son or daughter chooses personal freedom at the cost of family expectations. A leader balances honesty against harmony, truth against stability. In each case, the struggle is not about ignorance, but about responsibility.

Modern life intensifies Dharma Sankat because speed replaces reflection and validation replaces conscience. Decisions are often made to avoid discomfort rather than to uphold what sustains. The question subtly shifts from “What is right?” to “What is acceptable?” and in that shift, Dharma begins to erode.

Yet Dharma Sankat is not a failure of character. It is an invitation to deeper awareness. It asks for Yogastha Buddhi, a steady intelligence that can hold conflicting truths without collapsing into fear or escape. It demands flexibility in action while remaining anchored in principle, because Dharma survives not through rigidity, but through adaptation that sustains life and order.

In every age, Dharma Sankat tests whether action arises from convenience or conscience. When conscience leads, even painful choices preserve inner integrity. When it is ignored, even successful outcomes leave behind unrest. This is why Dharma remains relevant, not as an ancient rulebook, but as a living responsibility that accompanies every meaningful choice.

Where Dharma Becomes Personal
Dharma does not arrive with certainty or clarity. It arrives quietly, often when no option feels complete and no outcome feels safe. In those moments, life is not asking for correctness, approval, or success. It is asking for presence.

What makes Dharma difficult is not its complexity, but its demand for honesty. It asks that action emerge from awareness rather than habit, from responsibility rather than fear. This is why Dharma cannot be outsourced to rules, ideologies, or trends. It must be recognized inwardly and lived outwardly.

In a world that constantly rewards speed and certainty, choosing with awareness becomes a quiet act of courage. Dharma survives not because it resists change, but because it adapts without losing its centre. When action remains rooted in conscience, even imperfect choices retain dignity.

Perhaps Dharma is not something to be solved or mastered. Perhaps it is something to be returned to, again and again, whenever life places us at the edge of choice. I didn’t arrive at this understanding easily, and I still fail at it more often than I’d like.

धर्मो रक्षति रक्षितः
Dharma protects those who protect it.
